meta.title: Who really said "It takes two to speak the truth, — one to speak, and another to hear"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, it's really Thoreau. The line is from his 1849 book A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers, in the Wednesday chapter's passage on friendship.

author.name: Henry David Thoreau
author.heading: About Henry David Thoreau
author.bio: Henry David Thoreau was an American Transcendentalist writer best known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience. His first book, A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers (1849), grew out of a boating trip with his brother John and weaves travelogue together with digressive essays on friendship, poetry, and religion — the source of this line.

misattribution.heading: A note on wording
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare feel-good Thoreau lines that is actually his — so the issue isn’t who said it but how it’s reproduced.

items.why: Many databases render it with a colon — “It takes two to speak the truth: one to speak…” — but Thoreau’s text uses a comma and an em-dash: “the truth, — one to speak.” See the original text ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution is correct: it’s from Thoreau’s A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers ↗ (1849), “Wednesday.”

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Thoreau places the line in a passage arguing that friendship, not mere assertion, is what makes truth possible. Speaking the truth, for him, is not a solitary act of declaration but a shared one — it needs a listener generous enough to receive it.

The surrounding sentences frame a Friend as “one who incessantly pays us the compliment of expecting from us all the virtues,” making clear that the “hearing” half of truth is an act of trust and attention, not passivity.
